A checklist with three columns. Do I know what this is? Do I know what I'm supposed to do with it? Have I actually done it? Plenty of lines in a life get the first tick and stall there. Near the end of his first sermon, the Buddha describes his own checklist, the one he ran through before he would say he was awakened. Four truths, three looks each.

segments.voice: For each of the four truths, the Buddha describes knowing it in three turns. The first turn: this is the truth. This is dukkha. The second: this is what's to be done with it. Dukkha is to be understood. The third: it has been done. Dukkha has been understood. Then the same three for the arising: this is the arising; it's to be let go; it has been let go. For the ending: to be realized, and realized. For the path: to be developed, and developed. Four truths times three turns: twelve aspects. Then the striking line. The Buddha tells the five monks that as long as his knowledge of these three turns and twelve aspects wasn't fully clear, he didn't claim to be awakened. Only when all twelve were clear did he say it. That's honesty about his own path, built right into the first sermon. Then the story turns. As the sermon ends, one of the five, Kondañña, sees it. The sutta says the clear vision arose in him that whatever has the nature to arise has the nature to cease. And the Buddha says, Kondañña has understood. That, the sutta says, is how he got the name Aññasi Kondañña, Kondañña who understood. The sutta says the gods of the earth shouted that the wheel had been set rolling, and the cry passed up through the heavens. Some teachers today use the twelve as a map: knowing a truth, knowing its task, and doing it are three different things.

segments.voice: The Buddha is staying in a grove of simsapa trees near Kosambi. He picks up a few leaves and asks the monks: which are more, these in my hand or the leaves in the grove overhead? The leaves in the grove, they say, by far. In the same way, he says, the things I have directly known but not taught are far more. Then the part that's easy to skip. Why hasn't he taught them? Because they aren't beneficial. They don't belong to the basics of the holy life. They don't lead to letting go, to calm, to peace, to direct knowing, to awakening, to nibbana. And what has he taught? This is dukkha. This is its arising. This is its ending. This is the way. Because that does help. It leads to letting go, to calm, to peace, to awakening. So the handful isn't a random sample. It's a careful choice, and the filter is simple: does it help? The Buddha isn't hiding anything mysterious behind his back, or saying the rest of the forest is forbidden. He's a teacher who knows what a student needs, the way the cook knows her friend needs dinner. Fittingly, this sutta sits in the book of the four truths, the Buddha explaining why the last two weeks have been about four sentences and not four hundred. And it hands us a test for anything we read, watch, or worry about: does this lead to calm and freedom, or just to more noise?

346.title: The poisoned arrow
346.hook: a wounded man refuses treatment until he knows who shot him and why (MN 63)
346.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers in different schools tell the parable of the poisoned arrow to explain why the Buddha set certain metaphysical questions aside and focused on the four truths.

segments.voice: Yesterday: simsapa, the handful of leaves. The Buddha taught only what helps. Your line: only what helps.

A monk named Malunkyaputta is sitting alone, and he's annoyed. There are questions the Buddha has never answered. Is the world eternal, or not? Is it infinite, or finite? Is the soul the same as the body, or different? Does an awakened one exist after death, or not, or both, or neither? He makes up his mind: he'll demand answers, and if the Buddha won't give them, he'll give up the robe and go back to ordinary life. It's an ultimatum. The Buddha answers it with a story about an arrow.
screen: `A MONK, ANNOYED.` → `TEN BIG QUESTIONS.` → `ANSWER, OR I LEAVE.`

segments.voice: First, the Buddha asks him: did I ever say, come and live the holy life and I'll answer these for you? No, Malunkyaputta admits. Did you ever say, I'll live it only if you answer? No. Then the story. A man is shot with an arrow thickly smeared with poison. His friends and family rush to bring a surgeon. But the man says: I won't let this arrow be pulled out until I know who shot me. Was he a noble, a priest, a merchant, a worker? What's his name, his clan? Was he tall or short? Dark or golden-skinned? What village is he from? Was the bow a longbow or a crossbow? What was the bowstring made of? The shaft? Which bird's feathers were on it? That man would die, the Buddha says, and still not know. Whether the world is eternal or not, there is still birth, aging, death, sorrow and grief, and their ending is what he teaches. He left those ten questions undeclared because answering them isn't beneficial and doesn't lead to peace and awakening. What he has declared: this is dukkha, its arising, its ending, the way. He doesn't call the questions stupid, or forbid thinking about them. They're just not the urgent thing. And the list of feathers and bowstrings runs long enough that the man's priorities speak for themselves. The arrow is the hurt itself. The questions are everything a person might want settled before dealing with it.

347.title: The blind turtle
347.hook: a turtle surfacing once a century through a yoke adrift on the ocean: human birth is that rare (SN 56.48)
347.howItsDone: In Tibetan traditions especially, practitioners often reflect on the precious human life at the start of practice, sometimes recalling the image of the blind turtle and the yoke.

segments.voice: Yesterday: salla, the poisoned arrow. Treat the wound before asking who shot it. Your line: pull the arrow out.

The odds of a particular person being born are hard to even write down. Your parents had to meet, on that day, and their parents before them, back through every war and famine and missed train. People like to play with those numbers. The Buddha played with them too, only without numbers. He used an ocean, a wooden yoke with a single hole, and a turtle who can't see. It's a strange picture, and it sits in the book of the four truths for a reason.
screen: `THE ODDS OF BEING BORN.` → `AN OCEAN, A YOKE, A TURTLE.` → `IN THE BOOK OF THE FOUR TRUTHS.`

segments.voice: Here's the picture, from the Connected Discourses. Suppose someone threw into the great ocean a yoke, the wooden collar you'd put on an ox, with a single hole in it. And in that ocean a blind turtle comes up to the surface once every hundred years. Would the turtle, coming up, push its neck through the hole? Only after a very long time, the monks say, if ever. The neighboring sutta makes the scene bigger. Suppose the whole earth were one sheet of water. The east wind pushes the yoke west, the west wind pushes it east, the north wind south, the south wind north. It would be by chance, the monks say, that the turtle's neck went through. Just so, the Buddha says, it's by chance that someone is born human, by chance that a Buddha appears, by chance that the teaching shines in the world. And now all three have happened. Then the point lands: so effort should be made to understand this is dukkha, this is its arising, this is its ending, this is the way. The turtle isn't there to make anyone feel lucky, or anxious. It's there to make this hour feel valuable. Teachers, especially in Tibetan traditions, call it a precious human life: the time, the senses and the freedom to hear the teaching and practice it. The Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation, says it plainly: "Difficult (to obtain) is the conception of men, difficult is the life of mortals." Different schools read rebirth in their own ways. The sutta's own point is urgency.

348.title: This, because of that
348.hook: when this is, that is; from the arising of this, that arises (SN 12.21)
348.howItsDone: Buddhists study dependent arising as a central teaching in every school; Theravada monastics chant its formula, and Mahayana and Tibetan teachers often present it as the key to understanding emptiness.

You're snappish with someone at dinner. Why? Because you're tired. Why tired? You slept badly. Why? You were up late answering messages, because a deadline moved. Why did it move? Because someone else's plan fell through, because of their week, because of theirs. Pull on any single mood and you find a thread attached to other threads, all the way out. The Buddha put this into a formula so short it would fit on a fortune cookie.
screen: `SNAPPISH AT DINNER.` → `WHY? WHY? WHY?` → `A THREAD ATTACHED TO THREADS.`

segments.voice: The word is paticcasamuppada. Paticca means depending on, leaning on. Samuppada means arising together. Dependent arising, or dependent origination. In the Connected Discourses, book twelve, the Buddha gives it in four lines. When this is, that comes to be. With the arising of this, that arises. When this is not, that does not come to be. With the ending of this, that ends. No names, no gods, no story. Just a pattern. Here's why it matters. The four truths say dukkha has a cause, and that it can end. Dependent arising explains how both are possible. If dukkha just existed on its own, nothing could be done. But it leans on conditions. Change the conditions, and it changes. The third and fourth lines are the hopeful ones. There's a famous moment in the Long Discourses. Ananda tells the Buddha that dependent arising, though they say it's deep, seems perfectly clear to him. The Buddha stops him. Don't say that, Ananda. It is deep, and it looks deep, and because people don't understand it, they get tangled like a ball of string. So two things are true at once: it's simple enough to say over dinner, and deep enough to take a lifetime. Buddhist schools have unfolded it in different ways, some as a chain across lifetimes, some as the way every moment hangs together. The formula sits underneath them all.

349.title: The twelve links
349.hook: ignorance, formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the senses, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, becoming, birth, aging-and-death (SN 12.1)
349.howItsDone: In Tibetan monasteries the wheel of life is often painted near the entrance with the twelve links around its rim; in Theravada lands the links are chanted and studied, often following the commentaries' three-life reading.

segments.voice: Yesterday: paticcasamuppada, dependent arising. When this is, that comes to be. Your line: leans on conditions.

Near the entrance of a Tibetan temple, you may find a huge painted wheel held in the claws and teeth of a fierce figure. Around its outer rim run twelve small pictures. A blind person with a stick. A potter at his wheel. A monkey swinging through a tree. People in a boat. A house with windows. A couple embracing. A man with an arrow in his eye. Someone drinking. Someone picking fruit. A pregnant woman. A birth. An old body being carried away. It looks like a puzzle. It's a teaching.
screen: `A PAINTED WHEEL BY THE DOOR.` → `TWELVE SMALL PICTURES.` → `A PUZZLE THAT'S A TEACHING.`

segments.voice: The very first sutta in the book on dependent arising, in the Connected Discourses, lays the chain out. With ignorance as condition, there are formations. Then the links run on: consciousness; name-and-form, the mind and body together; the six senses; contact, where a sense meets its object; feeling, pleasant, painful or neither; craving; clinging; becoming; birth; and finally aging and death, with sorrow, grief and despair. Such, the sutta says, is the arising of this whole mass of dukkha. Now match them to the wheel. Ignorance is the blind person, feeling the way. Formations, the potter, the way past actions shape what comes. Consciousness, the monkey jumping from branch to branch. Name-and-form, the people in the boat, traveling together. The six senses, the house with its windows. Contact, the embrace. Feeling, the arrow in the eye. Craving is drinking, clinging is grabbing fruit, becoming is the pregnancy, then birth, then the body carried off. The paintings are a later Indian and Tibetan tradition; the suttas give only the list. The same sutta then runs the chain again as an ending: with the ending of ignorance, formations end, and so on, link by link, to the ending of this whole mass of dukkha. Buddhists read the chain in more than one way. The Theravada commentaries spread it across three lifetimes: past, present and future. Some teachers also read it moment by moment, in a single afternoon. Both readings are part of the living tradition.

350.title: Where the chain breaks
350.hook: between feeling and craving there is a gap where the chain can be cut
350.howItsDone: In several Buddhist meditation traditions, practitioners note feelings as pleasant, unpleasant or neutral as they arise, so that craving and aversion can be seen before they take hold.

segments.voice: Yesterday: nidana, the twelve links on the painted wheel, from ignorance to aging and death. Your line: twelve links.

Someone cuts in front of you in line. There's a hot flash of unpleasantness, right in the chest. That part is quick and nobody chose it. Then, in less than a blink, the second part arrives: the story, the glare, the rehearsed speech, the replay on the drive home. The two can blur into one event. They aren't one. Between them there's a seam, and some teachers point to it as the place in the twelve links where the chain can be cut.
screen: `SOMEONE CUTS IN LINE.` → `A HOT FLASH. THEN THE STORY.` → `BETWEEN THEM, A SEAM.`

segments.voice: Look at the middle of the chain. Contact gives rise to feeling: pleasant, painful or neither. Feeling gives rise to craving: want more, want it gone. The suttas don't use the word gap; that image comes from how some teachers apply the links. But the suttas do say a trained follower of the Buddha still feels. Still has a body, still meets heat and cold and rude people. What doesn't follow is the craving. So the link from feeling to craving isn't welded. The Buddha pictured it in a sutta called the Arrow, in the Connected Discourses, a different arrow from Malunkyaputta's. When an untrained person is touched by a painful feeling, he sorrows and laments and becomes distraught. He feels two pains, one in the body and one in the mind, like a man shot with one arrow and then shot again with a second. The trained person feels the first arrow and isn't hit by the second. The first arrow is feeling. The second is everything we pile on top. That's the seam, and it's where practice works: not by refusing to feel, but by meeting the feeling cleanly, so craving has nothing to grab. Now the week, from the top. Three turns: each truth known, its task known, its task done. A handful of leaves: only what helps. Salla: treat the wound before asking who shot it. Kacchapa: a rare human life. Dependent arising in four lines. Nidana, on the painted wheel. And today, the place to cut.
screen: `FEELING, THEN CRAVING.` · `THE TRAINED STILL FEEL.` · `THE FIRST ARROW AND THE SECOND.` · `THE WEEK, FROM THE TOP.` · then, large: `CUT BETWEEN.`

segments.voice: Sit still and wait for something to happen: an itch, a sound, an ache, a pleasant warmth. The moment you notice it, label it softly, pleasant, unpleasant or neither; that's the first arrow. Then watch with real curiosity for the next half-second, the lean toward or away, and if you see it, you've found the seam.
Vedana. The felt tone of an experience, pleasant, painful or neither, the link just before craving: the first arrow comes, and the second doesn't have to.
Your line: cut between. Met cleanly, a feeling leaves craving nothing to grab. Three hundred fifty days now.
